Nothing owns a competitor deliberately pricing below you as a market condition rather than an objection. Opinion shape. The argument to make, and it is the opposite of the usual add-more-value advice: before deciding anything, work out whether the competitor is cheaper or whether they are selling something smaller that looks the same from outside, because in most cases I have looked at it is the second, and the fix is describing the difference rather than defending the number. Then the three responses that exist, named honestly: match and change your cost base, hold and narrow who you sell to, or unbundle so there is a comparable cheap version of you on the shelf. Each has a real cost and the article should say what each one costs. Then the thing nobody says out loud: a competitor pricing below sustainable cost is a temporary condition and waiting it out is a legitimate strategy if your balance sheet can, and a losing one if it cannot, so the decision is about your cash rather than your positioning. Never rubbish a named company. Close with a straight opinion on which of the three is right for a business that cannot cut its costs.

The argument: in most small companies marketing and sales write promises that delivery has to keep, and nobody has been given authority to refuse, so the refusal happens anyway but late, badly, and by the most junior person in the chain. Give the practical shape without turning it into a process guide: who signs off a promise, what the standing list of things we do not do contains, and who tells the client. retired.angle: COVERAGE CHECKED against the section index and post bodies. b2b-demand-generation-vs-capture mentions review sites once as a capture channel. best-digital-marketing-agencies-2026 and marketing-agency-red-flags mention Clutch-style listings in passing. yelp-or-google-business-profile-which-first owns the Yelp-versus-GBP triage. my-competitor-is-buying-fake-reviews and the two negative-review posts own review handling. Nothing owns a directory or review site outranking you for your own name, which is the query here. The answer early and flatly: for your own brand name you can almost always fix this, and for category queries you often cannot and should stop trying. Separate the two cases, because the advice is opposite. For your own name, the usual causes are mechanical and fixable in an afternoon: no clear homepage title containing the business name, missing or wrong Organization schema with sameAs, a thin or missing about page, and the directory holding more inbound links than you do. For category queries like best plumber in a metro, the review site wins because it satisfies a comparison intent your single-vendor page structurally cannot, so the move is to be the best-looking entry inside that listing rather than to outrank it, and to measure the listing as a channel instead of as a competitor. The concrete middle: a short audit of what the directory has on its page about you that your own site does not. Close on the opinion worth arguing with, that for most local businesses the directory ranking above you is a distribution channel you are refusing to optimise because it offends you.
retired.audience: A US business owner who sees a directory above their own site in search results

retired.working_title: Which of your customers actually make you money?
retired.angle: COVERAGE CHECKED against the section index and post bodies. A grep for customer profitability, most profitable customer and which customers make you money returned ZERO hits, so this is clean ground. client-concentration-risk-small-business owns revenue dependence on one client and is the natural link. should-i-fire-a-client owns the decision to end a relationship and the real-hourly-rate test, so this post must not restate that test and should link it. marketing-budget-percentage-of-revenue owns headroom. Opinion shape. The argument: the client list ranked by revenue is the most misleading document in a service business, and almost every owner has one and nothing else. Make the case that profit per client and revenue per client are not correlated and are often inverted, because the accounts that pay most tend to demand the most governance, and the small ones that nobody manages are frequently the best margin. Then the part worth arguing with: this is a MARKETING problem rather than an accounting one, because once you know which shape of customer is profitable, the whole acquisition brief changes, and most firms are spending their budget attracting more of their worst cohort because that cohort is what the revenue list flatters. Give a method honestly, without inventing benchmarks: allocate the unbilled time, allocate the cost of the people who only exist because of that account, and be explicit that the number will be rough and rough is enough to change a decision. Close on the opinion that a firm which cannot name its most profitable customer type has no acquisition strategy, only an acquisition budget.
retired.audience: A US agency, consultancy or service business owner who has never run the numbers per client

retired.working_title: How much does a website cost in India?
retired.angle: COVERAGE CHECKED against the section index and post bodies. Nothing matched website cost at all. digital-marketing-consultant-cost-india and what-digital-marketing-actually-costs-in-india own marketing service pricing and the tenfold quote spread argument, so this post must not re-run that argument in the same shape and should link one of them. is-my-website-worth-rebuilding-or-just-fixing is US and owns the rebuild-versus-fix decision; website-launch-checklist is US and owns launch checks. why-did-my-website-get-slow-again owns performance. Clear ground. Practical and specific, in rupees throughout. Do not invent a price table: gather real current ranges from named Indian sources or frame as a range from experience, and say which it is. The useful structure is not a price list but a list of what actually moves the number, because the reader's real question is whether the quote in front of them is reasonable: how many templates versus how many unique page designs, who writes the copy, whether the content is migrated or retyped, forms and where the enquiry lands, payments, and who owns the hosting and the domain afterwards. Then the three cost traps I would check in any Indian quote: the website built on a page builder the agency controls, the copy left to the client and therefore never written, and the annual maintenance charge that exists to re-sell the same work. Concrete middle: a short list of questions to ask before signing, each with what a good answer sounds like. Close with the honest point that the cheapest usable site for a small business in India is usually cheaper than people expect and the expensive mistake is almost never the build price.
retired.audience: An Indian small business owner holding two or three website quotes
